items.title: Daphne Zuniga Addresses Future of 'Melrose Place' Podcast Amid Lengthy Pause
items.summary:
Daphne Zuniga is offering a rare update on her Melrose Place rewatch podcast with Courtney Thorne-Smith and Laura Leighton amid its ongoing pause.

“We did the first season and then our schedules all kind of split up,” Zuniga, 64, explained during an exclusive interview with Us on the set of Fox’s Celebrity Weakest Link . 

Zuniga hinted that they also “didn’t get the followers that we really needed.”

“We had passionate [listeners], but iHeartRadio had a quota and they just needed to make that,” she recalled about the podcast, which premiered in summer 2024. “And we’re like, ‘What about that theory of things will build?’ Then [Courtney and Laura] got busy. I was off shooting Spaceballs: The New One and everyone’s [working on something].”

'Melrose Place’ Stars on Plans to Modernize the Reboot for the Next Generation 

The actress, who played Jo Reynolds, didn’t rule out returning to the podcast project. “But we did get a call about would we want to revisit it? That was [a few] months ago,” she said. “So when things calm down, we might [return].”

She continued: “And it was just getting good because Melrose Place really got good when you get into all the big drama stuff, which was just happening at the end of the first season.”

Melrose Place , which ran from 1992 to 1999 , followed a group of young adults living in an apartment complex in West Hollywood. After filming her episode of Celebrity Weakest Link — alongside fellow ’90s stars Mario Cantone, Zac Hanson, Jasmine Guy, Jonathan Lipnicki, Sisqo, Kel Mitchell and Stephen Baldwin — Zuniga had a few suggestions for which…
items.t: Daphne Zuniga Addresses Future of 'Melrose Place' Podcast Amid Lengthy Pause

items.title: Jen Affleck Addresses Nail Technician Leaking Her Pregnancy Before Divorce
items.summary:
Jen Affleck ‘s nail tech Kortney Poulson broke her silence about allegedly leaking her client’s pregnancy — and the reality star quickly weighed in. 

During season 1 of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County , which is streaming now, Affleck, 27, learned on camera that Poulson had told others that the Hulu personality was pregnant with baby No. 4.

“I just wanna briefly address everything that’s being said online. Unfortunately, there’s a lot of context that is missing from the show,” Poulson said in an Instagram video on Saturday, November 14. “I am accepting that I’m going to have to live with people forming opinions about me without knowing the full story.”

Poulson made it clear that she was on good terms with Affleck.

Mormon Wives' Jen Affleck Reveals Why She Filed for Divorce From Zac Affleck

items.title: Glenn Close Recalls Growing Up in a Cult as She Receives Honorary Oscar

The All’s Fair actress, 79, received an honorary Oscar at the 2026 Governors Awards on Sunday, November 15, in the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood in Los Angeles.

Close was visibly emotional as she accepted the award, discussing her life growing up in what she described as a cult.

“It’s very difficult for me to process this incredible honor, because the truth is, I carry the epigenome of an outsider,” she said . “From the ages of 7 to 22, I was under the thumb of a very restrictive cult — don’t look at yourself in a mirror, no flirting, dress this way, talk this way, say it’s OK when your parents are routinely sent away from you for months on end. It meant that I was always on the outside looking in.”

Where Is Her Oscar?! Glenn Close Through the Years: Her Life in Photos 

Close went on to dedicate her award to her daughter and fellow actress, Annie Starke , and spoke about her previous brushes with Academy Awards glory.

“As an outsider, I was never worried about whether I was going to win or not, though some years I thought I might have a chance,” she said. “I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room. Over the past 43 years, I’ve been in the room eight times … not looking in the window, but in the room, part of this extraordinary community. So to be in this room tonight, embraced by the people who have consistently inspired me, whose work has sustained and challenged me and only made me want to be better, is the greatest honor of all.”

items.title: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood
items.summary:
After years of celebrity interviews, I have learned not to be fooled by the allure of fame. We never really know them – we know what they want us to know

As I sat in Southwark crown court, listening to the final day of Russell Brand’s trial, there was one subject that came up repeatedly, invoked as often by his defence as the prosecution. I don’t mean sex or coercion, but fame. It ran through every victim impact statement and loomed so large in the courtroom that it felt as if it was almost on trial itself.

I’m an entertainment journalist who has been covering celebrities for more than 20 years – as long as Brand has been one – and I have written about him at various stages of his career. But I went to Southwark crown court as a member of the public who wanted to see justice done. For the women he had hurt, for the ones who couldn’t get as far as the courtroom, and for all of us who came of age at a time when rape culture was so fast and furious that young women mistook it for a joke that we were in on. In the age of lads’ mags, sex felt cheapened, yet somehow we were the ones who ended up paying for this. So it was doubly strange to sit in court and feel somehow complicit in it - in how this media culture had encouraged Russell Brand.

items.t: I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows | Sophie Heawood

He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.”

He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks.

items.title: Years of onscreen jokes suggest Walliams’ reputation was ‘in plain sight’ within industry, insider says
items.summary:
References raise questions over whether claims about bankable stars have been ignored by entertainment industry

The comedy sketch opens in a doctor’s office, with a trouserless David Walliams apparently being treated for a fictional sexually transmitted disease. The doctor tells him it is bad news and he needs to contact “everyone you’ve been intimate with over the last year”.

The camera closes in on the comedian’s shocked expression before he gasps: “Everyone?”
